1.pericope_label: The clothes of service and the holy garments; the ephod and the beating of the gold into thread

schools.summary: Report the rabbinic reading that the cloths of service were coverings for the vessels in transit rather than vestments, and the rabbinic recipe for the gold thread; and defend the chapter’s repetition as neither trivial nor pompous, the vestments existing to set before the eye what faith should see in Christ, with the sevenfold refrain counted as a device to awaken attention.

Take the phrase “clothes of service” as the lesson of the passage — honour carries service with it, and holy garments were made to work in — then read the whole vesture typologically of Christ the high priest and of believers as spiritual priests; and count the paragraphs that close with the refrain, noting that no earlier account of the tabernacle repeats it so.

Carry the same lesson and the same typology of the high priest and of the righteousness of saints; refuse the inference that beating gold into plates proves a backward metallurgy, since the people had harder arts already and the work may simply have wanted a more solid figure; and route the reader back to the earlier chapters for the colours and the ephod.

Refer the disputed phrases to the earlier notes rather than re-arguing them; and treat the beaten gold as evidence about technique — a method mentioned nowhere else, implying a ruder state of the art than expected, with the gold added by embroidery to an already patterned fabric, as Egyptian practice shows.

debates: What the “cloths of service” were — coverings for the sanctuary vessels in transit, on the rabbinic argument from the absence of linen (Gill), or garments actually worn in ministry (the view Gill reports against it, and the sense Henry and Wesley assume).

What the beaten gold proves about Israelite metallurgy: Ellicott infers a ruder state of the art than expected, Clarke expressly refuses the inference and explains the method by the requirements of the figure instead.
How many times the refrain “as the Lord commanded Moses” governs the chapter — Calvin says seven, Henry counts six paragraphs and lists their verses.
Whether the elaborate vesture is to be expounded as type (Henry, Wesley, Calvin) or as historical craft to be explained from comparative evidence (Clarke, Ellicott).
outliers: Calvin alone turns the description into polemic, contrasting the priestly vesture with the vestments of the Roman clergy as pomp calculated to dazzle.
Clarke alone argues from what the Israelites could already do to what they must have been able to do, against the plain implication of the verse.
Gill alone preserves the rabbinic recipe for the composite thread, down to the count of twenty-eight.
Henry alone remarks that no earlier account of the tabernacle’s furniture repeats the refrain as this one does.

6.pericope_label: The onyx stones, the breastplate and its four rows of stones

schools.summary: Offer the Egyptian pebble as a possible identification of the onyx without settling it, and refer the breastplate and its twelve stones back to the instructions where they were described.
Refer the memorial character of the shoulder-stones to the note on the corresponding instruction, treating the execution narrative as adding nothing to be argued.

debates: What stone the onyx of the shoulder-pieces was — Clarke raises the Egyptian pebble as a possibility and leaves it unsettled.
Whether the execution narrative calls for its own exposition or is to be read against the instructions of chapter 28, which is how both voices here handle it.
outliers: Clarke alone offers a mineralogical identification, and offers it as a conjecture.

23.pericope_label: The opening of the robe, and the pomegranates and bells upon its hem

schools.summary: Explain the bound opening of the robe by the hauberk of medieval Europe, describing its construction and then deriving it from Persian use rather than the reverse.

Correct the Authorised rendering of the pomegranates, taking the three colours as twisted into one thread rather than set beside a separate linen, and refer the purpose of the bells to the instruction that prescribed them.

debates: Whether the pomegranates were of three colours plus linen, as the English implies, or of the three colours twisted together, as Ellicott renders the Hebrew.

Whether a medieval European mail shirt is a serviceable comparison for the neck of the priestly robe, and in which direction the armour travelled — Clarke has the crusaders borrowing it from the Persians.
outliers: Clarke alone reaches outside the ancient world for his comparison, and alone traces the borrowing from Asia into Europe rather than assuming a European original.

27.pericope_label: The tunics, the turban and caps, the drawers, the girdle, and the plate of the holy crown

schools.summary: Correct four Authorised renderings in succession — tunics for coats, turban for mitre, caps for goodly bonnets, drawers for linen breeches — assigning each garment to Aaron or to his sons, and note that the girdle is described more fully here than in the instructions themselves.

Set the golden plate beside the crowns and tiaras worn by priests on Persian and Egyptian monuments and the laurel crowns of Greek priests and priestesses, who were styled crown-bearers for the practice.

debates: Whether the Authorised vocabulary for the priestly dress is accurate — Ellicott replaces mitre, bonnets and breeches with turban, caps and drawers throughout.
Whether the execution narrative merely repeats the instructions: Ellicott observes that the girdle is described more fully here than where it was commanded.
How the golden plate is to be understood — by reference to the instruction that prescribed it (Ellicott) or by comparison with the crowned priesthoods of Persia, Egypt and Greece (Clarke).
outliers: Ellicott alone distributes the garments between Aaron and his sons item by item.
Clarke alone treats the crown as a piece of general ancient priestly costume and gathers monumental and Greek evidence for it.

32.pericope_label: The work finished and brought to Moses; the inspection and the blessing

schools.summary: Account for the speed of the work by unanimity, divine teaching of the workmen and prepared hearts in the people; make the submission of the finished work to Moses a lesson in humility and subjection; and divide the blessing into commendation and prayer, explaining at length why no wages were owed.

Repeat the five months and the reasons for the despatch; and refer the exactness to the command about the pattern, taking Moses’ circumstantial repetition of every detail as his own evidence that he had conscientiously kept the directions given him.

Note that the parts were brought separately and reviewed in the order commanded; read the summary as declaring that no part of the building was impaired by any admixture; and deny that the blessing was a private prayer at all, making it a promise of reward from an unimpeachable witness, calculated to give the people confidence.

Attend to the inventory rather than the ceremony — the shewbread, oil and incense delivered with the vessels, so that daily worship could begin at once — and identify the vail in the list as the one screening the most holy place from sight.

debates: What the blessing was: commendation together with prayer (Henry, and Wesley in the same terms), or not a prayer at all but an authoritative promise of reward (Calvin).
Why nothing is said of wages — Henry gives three reasons why none were due, where the others do not raise the question.

Where the interest of the passage lies: in the workmen’s submission and the moral of it (Henry), in the purity of the executed work (Calvin), or in the completeness of the stores handed over, which made the daily service possible immediately (Keil).
Whether Moses’ own circumstantial repetition of the details is evidence about Moses, as Clarke takes it, or simply the form of the record.
outliers: Calvin alone refuses to read the blessing as prayer, and turns it into a public guarantee addressed to the people rather than to God.
Henry alone raises the question of payment and answers it, and alone rebukes the critic who cannot approve a work without finding a fault in it.
Keil alone observes that the consumable stores were delivered with the furniture, so that nothing further was needed before worship began.

37.pericope_label: The candlestick and its lamps, the altars and the vessels of service

schools.summary: Take “the lamps to be set in order” as the daily duty of trimming and fresh oiling against the evening lighting, referring it to the standing ordinance about the lamp, and leave the candlestick itself to the earlier description.

Render the same clause as a noun, “the lamps of arrangement,” and refer it to the disposition of the lamps in a single row, comparing the rows of shewbread; and gloss “vessels of service” from the place where the term was defined, before closing with Moses’ examination and blessing.

debates: What “the lamps to be set in order” means — the daily trimming and oiling of the lamps for the evening lighting (Clarke), or the arrangement of the lamps in a single row upon the candlestick (Ellicott).
Whether the clause describes the object as delivered or the ministry it was destined for, which is what the two renderings decide between.
outliers: Ellicott alone treats the phrase as a construct noun and looks to the shewbread for the parallel.
Clarke alone reads the clause forward into the priest’s daily service rather than back into the description of the finished work.

41.pericope_label: The cloths of service and the holy garments delivered to Moses

schools.summary: Remove the conjunction the English supplies and make the second and third clauses explanatory of the first, so that “cloths of service” is the heading under which the garments of Aaron and his sons are listed rather than a separate class beside them, referring the phrase to the same note used at the head of the chapter; or else pass over the grammar and take the verse as the hinge into the blessing, grounding that blessing in the people’s liberality and in their finishing the work in under half a year.

debates: Whether the verse lists three classes of thing, as the Authorised “and” implies, or one class with its explanation, as Ellicott’s reading of the unpointed clauses requires.
What Moses’ blessing rested on — Keil grounds it in the readiness of the givers and the speed of the workmen rather than in the accuracy of the work he had just inspected.
outliers: Ellicott alone treats the verse as a textual crux and ties his answer to his reading of the same phrase in the first verse of the chapter.
Keil alone dates the whole undertaking, putting it at rather less than half a year on the reckoning from the date of the tabernacle’s erection.

43.pericope_label: Moses inspects the finished work and blesses the people

schools.summary: Credit the exactness of the work to the Spirit’s filling of the workmen rather than to the inspection; extend the blessing to the givers as well as the builders; and supply the traditional form of the blessing from the Targum and from Jarchi.

Distinguish praise from prayer in the blessing and defend the first sense lexically and by an example of ancient courtesy between master and servant; argue that no wages were due because the workmen wrought for themselves and were already fed and clothed from heaven; and read the tabernacle as a type of the human nature of Christ, resting the reading on the Word made flesh pitching his tent among us.
Take the inspection as a comparison with the pattern and the blessing as the expression, once Moses was satisfied, of his own approval and of God’s.

debates: What “blessed them” means — commendation for skill and fidelity, intercessory prayer, or both together, with Clarke defending the first sense lexically and Wesley insisting on the second as well.
Who was blessed: the artificers only, or the whole people who had contributed (Clarke, Gill).

Whether the accuracy of the work is evidence about the inspector or about the workmen — Clarke makes Moses the superintendent who supplied the pattern, Gill and Wesley credit the Spirit’s guidance of the workmen’s hands.
Whether the tabernacle is to be read as a type of the incarnate Christ, which only Clarke argues here.
outliers: Gill alone preserves a form of the blessing, from the Targum of Jonathan and from Jarchi.
Clarke alone defends the word “blessed” in the sense of praise by appeal to an earlier note and to the greeting of Boaz and his reapers.
Wesley alone raises the question of wages and answers it from the manna and the unworn clothing.
Clarke alone builds the incarnation typology, and alone ends by turning the passage into a direct question to the reader.
